title: Mosaic: Harnessing the Micro-Architectural Resources of Servers in Serverless Environments
problem: Modern server-class processors suffer from inefficient utilization in serverless environments due to frequent context switches within function invocations and high core oversubscription, causing functions to lose micro-architectural state in caches, TLBs, and branch predictors.
motivation: Serverless computing requires efficient resource utilization to optimize cloud provider infrastructure for the increasingly popular lightweight function execution model.
method: Mosaic works by dividing up the CPU's performance-boosting hardware—caches (fast memory that stores frequently used data), TLBs (hardware that translates memory addresses), and branch predictors (hardware that guesses which direction code will jump)—into separate partitions assigned to individual functions. When the CPU switches between functions, each function's partition stays intact instead of being overwritten, so it keeps the benefit of cached data and correct predictions. Inactive partitions are put into low-power mode to save energy. A scheduler then smartly adjusts how much of each resource each function gets based on what it actually needs.
key_novelty: The core idea is to partition the CPU's performance-boosting hardware per function instead of sharing it globally, so each function preserves its hardware state when the CPU switches to another task.
contributions: MosaicCPU processor architecture with partitioned micro-architectural tiles for serverless workloads
